## Theorem

Every Lie group homeomorphic to the $n$-dimensional torus $\mathbb{T}^n$ is abelian (in fact, isomorphic to the standard torus $\mathbb{R}^n/\mathbb{Z}^n$).

## Proof

Let $G$ be a Lie group with $G \cong_{\text{top}} \mathbb{T}^n$. Then $G$ is compact and connected, and $\pi_1(G)\cong\mathbb{Z}^n$.

**Step 1. Structure of the universal cover.** Let $\widetilde G$ be the universal cover of $G$, with covering map $p:\widetilde G\to G$, and let $\Gamma=\ker p\cong\pi_1(G)\cong\mathbb{Z}^n$, a discrete central subgroup. Since $G$ is compact, its Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ is a *compact* Lie algebra, which decomposes as
$$\mathfrak g = \mathfrak z(\mathfrak g)\oplus[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g],$$
where $[\mathfrak g,\mathfrak g]$ is compact semisimple. Consequently
$$\widetilde G \cong \mathbb{R}^m \times K,$$
where $m=\dim\mathfrak z(\mathfrak g)$ and $K$ is compact, simply connected, and semisimple.

**Step 2. Locating $\Gamma$.** Since $\Gamma$ is central in $\widetilde G$, we have
$$\Gamma\subset Z(\widetilde G)=\mathbb{R}^m\times Z(K).$$
The center $Z(K)$ of a compact, simply connected, semisimple Lie group is **finite**. Since $\Gamma\cong\mathbb{Z}^n$ is torsion-free, the projection
$$\pi:\mathbb{R}^m\times Z(K)\to\mathbb{R}^m$$
restricts to an **injective** map on $\Gamma$ (its kernel is $\Gamma\cap(\{0\}\times Z(K))$, a finite subgroup of a torsion-free group, hence trivial). Thus $\Lambda:=\pi(\Gamma)$ is a discrete subgroup of $\mathbb{R}^m$ isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}^n$, i.e. a lattice of rank $n$, so $n\le m$.

**Step 3. Trivializing the $K$–component of $\Gamma$.** For each $\lambda\in\Lambda$ there is a unique $z(\lambda)\in Z(K)$ with $(\lambda,z(\lambda))\in\Gamma$, and $\lambda\mapsto z(\lambda)$ is a homomorphism $\Lambda\to Z(K)\subset K$. Since $\mathbb{R}^m$ is simply connected, every homomorphism $\Lambda\to K$ extends to a (smooth) homomorphism $\psi:\mathbb{R}^m\to K$ (lift the induced Lie-algebra map). Define
$$\Phi:\mathbb{R}^m\times K\to\mathbb{R}^m\times K,\qquad (v,k)\mapsto\bigl(v,\,\psi(v)^{-1}k\bigr).$$
This is a Lie-group automorphism, and
$$\Phi(\lambda,z(\lambda))=(\lambda,\psi(\lambda)^{-1}z(\lambda))=(\lambda,z(\lambda)^{-1}z(\lambda))=(\lambda,e),$$
so $\Phi(\Gamma)=\Lambda\times\{e\}$. Hence, as Lie groups,
$$G\cong(\mathbb{R}^m\times K)/(\Lambda\times\{e\})\cong(\mathbb{R}^m/\Lambda)\times K.$$

**Step 4. Compactness forces $m=n$.** The factor $\mathbb{R}^m/\Lambda$ is compact iff $\Lambda$ spans $\mathbb{R}^m$, i.e. $\operatorname{rank}\Lambda=m$. Since $\operatorname{rank}\Lambda=n$ and $G$ is compact, we get $m=n$. Thus
$$G\cong\mathbb{T}^n\times K$$
as Lie groups (with $\mathbb{R}^n/\Lambda\cong\mathbb{T}^n$).

**Step 5. Homotopy forces $K$ trivial.** The torus $\mathbb{T}^n$ is a $K(\mathbb{Z}^n,1)$: all its higher homotopy groups vanish, in particular $\pi_3(\mathbb{T}^n)=0$. On the other hand, for any nontrivial compact, simply connected, semisimple Lie group $K$ (i.e. with at least one simple factor), a classical theorem of Bott gives
$$\pi_3(K)\cong\mathbb{Z}^{\,r},\qquad r=\#\{\text{simple factors of }K\}\ge 1.$$
Therefore $\pi_3(G)=\pi_3(\mathbb{T}^n\times K)=\pi_3(K)$, which is nonzero whenever $K\neq\{e\}$. But $G\cong_{\text{top}}\mathbb{T}^n$ forces $\pi_3(G)=0$. Hence $K=\{e\}$.

**Conclusion.** With $K$ trivial,
$$G\cong\mathbb{R}^n/\Lambda\cong\mathbb{T}^n,$$
the standard torus, which is abelian. $\blacksquare$
